t:
Subsection (b) of the first section of the Act approved June 6, 1958 (D.C. Code, sec. 9–220(b)), is amended to read as follows:


“(b)

(1) 
To assist in financing the cost of constructing facilities required for activities financed by the general fund of the District, the Commissioners are hereby authorized to accept loans for the District from the United States Treasury, and the Secretary of the Treasury is hereby authorized to lend to the Commissioners such sums as may hereafter be appropriated for such purpose, except that no loan made under this subsection after June 30, 1967, shall cause the amount which is required to be paid in any fiscal year out of the general fund of the District as principal and interest on the aggregate indebtedness of the District to exceed—

“(A) 
in the case of an amount required to be paid in a fiscal year ending in 1968, 1969, or 1970, 6 per centum of the general revenue of the District which the Commissioners estimate will be credited to the general fund of the District during such fiscal year; or


“(B) 
in the case of an amount required to be paid in a fiscal year ending after June 30, 1970, 6 per centum of the general revenue of the District credited to the general fund of the District for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1970.



“(2) 
For purposes of paragraph (1) of this subsection, the term ‘general revenue of the District’ means the sum of—

“(A) 
the tax revenues of the District, including but not limited to the revenues (including penalties and interest) derived from the following taxes: (i) taxes imposed on real and tangible personal property, (ii) sales and gross receipts taxes, (iii) taxes on the incomes of individuals, corporations, and unincorporated businesses, (iv) real estate deed recordation taxes, and (v) inheritance and estate taxes;


“(B) 
proceeds from the motor vehicle registration fees collected under section 3 of title IV of the District of Columbia Revenue Act of 1937 (D.C. Code, sec. 40–103); and


“(C) 
the amount of the appropriation authorized by section 1 of article VI of the District of Columbia Revenue Act of 1947.



“(3) 
The appropriation of any loan made under this subsection shall not be construed to alter or to eliminate the procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation provided in the National Capital Planning Act of 1952 (D.C. Code, sec. 1–1001 et seq.). $50,000,000 of the principal amount of the loans authorized to be made to the Commissioners under this subsection shall be utilized to carry out the purposes of the National Capital Transportation Act of 1965 (D.C. Code, secs. 1–1404, 1–1421—1–1426); and $40,000,000 of the principal amount of such loans shall be utilized to carry out the purposes of the District of Columbia Public Education Act (Public Law 89–791).


“(4) 
Any loan made under this subsection shall be in addition to any other loans heretofore or hereafter made to the Commissioners for any other purpose, and when advanced shall be deposited in the Treasury of the United States to the credit of the general fund of the District.”

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the reference to "consultation, advice, and recommendation" makes this participation. That clause is only a savings provision that leaves procedures in a different statute untouched; it does not itself create or require any consultation with outside parties. The rest of the section authorizes Treasury loans to the District Commissioners, sets debt-service limits, and earmarks loan funds, which is a financing arrangement rather than outside involvement in a federal decision.
fable.s: The appropriation of any loan made under this subsection shall not be construed to alter or to eliminate the procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation provided in the National Capital Planning Act of 1952

qwen_block.w: This section is a savings clause that preserves existing procedures from another act (the National Capital Planning Act of 1952). It does not itself establish a new participation mechanism, nor does it describe the specific nature of those preserved procedures. Without evidence that the preserved procedures involve outside parties (as opposed to internal federal coordination or congressional reporting), this section does not meet the definition of participation. The text merely references other laws without detailing the participatory elements.
qwen_block.s: The appropriation of any loan made under this subsection shall not be construed to alter or to eliminate the procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation provided in the National Capital Planning Act of 1952 (D.C. Code, sec. 1–1001 et seq.).

opus.w: This section authorizes Treasury loans to the District Commissioners and caps how much debt the District can carry. The only procedural language is a savings clause stating that the loans don't change existing National Capital Planning Act procedures. That clause neither creates nor requires any consultation with parties outside the government. The consultation it preserves is mainly between government planning bodies, so the mention of 'consultation, advice, and recommendation' is not enough to make this outside-party participation.
opus.s: The appropriation of any loan made under this subsection shall not be construed to alter or to eliminate the procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation provided in the National Capital Planning Act of 1952 (D.C. Code, sec. 1–1001 et seq.).
opus.b:
I'm labelling this **No**, with moderate confidence (0.68).

**The tempting reading:** Paragraph (3) mentions "procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation" under the National Capital Planning Act. That looks like a participation process.

**Why it fails:** The clause only says the loans won't change those existing procedures. It doesn't create, require or recommend any new consultation with outside parties. The consultation it refers to also appears to run between government bodies: the District Commissioners and the National Capital Planning Commission. In 1967, the District Commissioners were presidential appointees. The rest of the section is about Treasury loans, debt limits and how the money is used.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes loans from the U.S. Treasury to the District of Columbia Commissioners. While it references existing consultation procedures in the National Capital Planning Act, it does not itself establish or require any new participation process. The reference is merely a savings clause ensuring existing laws remain in effect, not a mandate for new outside-party involvement in the decision to make the loans.
qwen_chat.s: The appropriation of any loan made under this subsection shall not be construed to alter or to eliminate the procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation provided in the National Capital Planning Act of 1952 (D.C. Code, sec. 1–1001 et seq.).
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: The text mentions "procedures for consultation, advice, and recommendation" in subsection (3), which might suggest participation. However, these procedures are part of the "National Capital Planning Act of 1952," a separate statute. This section merely states that the new loan authority does not *alter or eliminate* those existing procedures. It does not itself establish or require any new participation process. Furthermore, the "Commissioners" of the District of Columbia (at the time this law was written) were federal appointees, making them part of the federal government structure, so their internal consultations are not "outside" participation. The core action here is the authorization of loans from the Treasury to the District, which is a financial transaction, not a participatory decision-making process involving the public or outside entities.
